October 2, 2026

Lip injuries rank among the most common facial traumas seen in emergency departments, caused by everything from playground falls to car accidents to dog bites. The good news is that lips heal remarkably well compared to skin elsewhere on the body, thanks to an exceptionally rich blood supply and the unique biology of oral tissue. That said, proper first aid in the first minutes matters, and certain types of lip wounds need professional repair to avoid lasting cosmetic problems. Here is what you need to know about caring for a lip injury from the moment it happens through full recovery.

What to Do in the First Few Minutes

Lip injuries bleed a lot. The lips receive blood from a dense network of arteries running just a few millimeters below the surface, so even a small cut can produce dramatic bleeding that looks worse than it is. Your first priority is to control that bleeding by applying firm, steady pressure with a clean cloth or gauze. Hold it for at least ten minutes without peeking, since lifting the cloth too soon restarts the clotting process.

Once bleeding slows, gently clean the wound with clean running water. If the cut is on the outside of the lip, a mild soap around (not directly inside) the wound helps remove debris. For cuts inside the mouth, a gentle rinse with clean water works. Remove any visible dirt, gravel, or fragments, but do not probe deeply into the wound yourself. Apply a cold compress or wrapped ice pack to the area for ten to fifteen minutes to reduce swelling. Over-the-counter pain relief like ibuprofen or acetaminophen can help with both pain and inflammation.

A minor lip cut that is shallow, stops bleeding with pressure, and does not cross the border between the colored part of the lip and the surrounding skin will usually heal fine on its own with basic wound care. Keep it clean, avoid picking at any scab that forms, and apply a thin layer of petroleum jelly to keep the wound moist while it closes.

When You Need to See a Doctor

Not every lip injury can be managed at home. Several features signal that a wound needs professional attention, sometimes urgently.

The most critical landmark on the lip is the vermilion border, the sharp line where the red-colored lip meets the surrounding skin. Lacerations that cross this border require precise alignment during closure. Even a one- to two-millimeter mismatch at the vermilion border is visible at conversational distance, so these wounds should be repaired by a clinician experienced in facial suturing. Lacerations involving more than about a quarter of the lip’s width are particularly challenging and prone to deformity if not carefully repaired.
1
PubMed Central. 
Lip Laceration and Vermilion Border Repair

Other reasons to seek care include wounds that go all the way through the lip (entering the mouth), any wound with visible muscle or fat, injuries caused by animal or human bites, lacerations with embedded debris you cannot remove, wounds that will not stop bleeding after twenty minutes of direct pressure, and any injury associated with loose or broken teeth. If the wound is on a young child who cannot keep the area clean or still, professional closure is usually the safer choice.

How Lip Lacerations Are Repaired

When a lip laceration needs stitches, the approach a clinician takes depends on the wound’s depth, location, and whether it crosses key landmarks.

Before anything else, the wound needs effective numbing. Traditional local anesthesia, where numbing medication is injected directly into the wound edges, can swell the tissue and distort important landmarks like the vermilion border. Many emergency and plastic surgery providers now prefer nerve blocks instead. A mental nerve block numbs the lower lip, and an infraorbital nerve block numbs the upper lip, both without injecting into the wound itself.
2
PubMed. 
Lip and perioral trauma
 A study comparing the two approaches found that nerve blocks required roughly half the anesthetic volume, produced significantly lower pain scores, and preserved the natural tissue contours far better than direct injection.
3
PubMed. 
Aesthetic Unit Preservation in Emergency Facial Lacerations: A Prospective Evaluation of Landmark-Based Nerve Blocks

The lips consist of three distinct layers: outer skin, the orbicularis oris muscle in the middle, and inner oral mucosa. A full-thickness laceration, one that goes all the way through, requires repair of each layer separately. The clinician typically starts by precisely aligning the vermilion border with the first suture, since that landmark is the most visible. Muscle is then repaired to restore function, followed by closure of the inner mucosal layer and the outer skin. Intraoral sutures are usually made with absorbable material that dissolves on its own, while outer stitches on the skin side are typically removed after four to five days to prevent visible suture marks from forming.
4
Emergency Medicine Clinics of North America. 
Lacerations of the Mouth – Section: Wound Dressing and Care

Why Lips Heal Better Than Most Skin

If you have ever noticed that a cut inside your mouth seems to vanish in days while a scrape on your arm lingers for weeks, you are not imagining things. The oral mucosa, the moist tissue lining the inside of your mouth and the inner surface of your lips, heals faster and with less scarring than skin almost anywhere else on the body.
5
PubMed Central. 
The Bigger Picture: Why Oral Mucosa Heals Better Than Skin

Several factors drive this advantage. The oral environment stays consistently moist, which promotes cell migration across the wound surface. Saliva contains growth factors and antimicrobial compounds that actively support healing. The immune response in oral tissue resolves more quickly, meaning less prolonged inflammation and less of the excessive collagen buildup that creates thick scars. Research comparing matched wounds in skin and oral mucosa found significantly reduced scar formation in the mouth at both the visible and microscopic level, with skin wounds showing higher levels of collagen-producing cells and scar-associated proteins.
6
PubMed. 
Wound healing in oral mucosa results in reduced scar formation as compared with skin: evidence from the red Duroc pig model and humans
 Oral mucosal wounds also showed faster resolution of inflammation and better control of the cells responsible for wound contraction, both key reasons why mouth wounds heal with minimal scarring.
7
PubMed. 
Scarless healing of oral mucosa is characterized by faster resolution of inflammation and control of myofibroblast action compared to skin wounds in the red Duroc pig model

The outer skin surface of the lip does not share all of these advantages, so cuts on the external lip side heal more like regular skin wounds. Still, the lip’s outstanding blood supply gives even outer lip wounds a healing edge over lacerations on less vascular body parts. Both the superior and inferior labial arteries run through the lip tissue at an average depth of roughly five millimeters, and the arteries course most commonly through the submucosal plane, keeping the tissue well-oxygenated during repair.
8
SpringerLink (Aesthetic Plastic Surgery). 
The Blood Supply of the Lips: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

Animal Bites to the Lip

Dog bites are a leading cause of lip lacerations, and the lips are the most commonly affected site in head-and-face bite injuries.
9
PubMed. 
Animal bite injuries to the head: 132 cases
 Bite wounds carry a higher infection risk than clean-cut lacerations because animal mouths harbor a mix of bacteria that gets driven deep into the tissue. Despite that risk, current practice favors immediate primary closure of facial bite wounds rather than leaving them open to heal on their own. Thorough wound cleaning and irrigation, combined with antibiotic prophylaxis, yields good cosmetic results with a low infection rate.
10
PubMed Central. 
Animal Inflicted Maxillofacial Injuries: Treatment Modalities and Our Experience
 The antibiotic of first choice for bite wounds is typically amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, which covers the common bacteria found in animal saliva.
9
PubMed. 
Animal bite injuries to the head: 132 cases

If you are bitten, do not wait to see how it looks. Bite wounds to the face should be evaluated promptly. In addition to infection risk, the crushing and tearing nature of a bite can damage underlying muscle and nerves in ways that are not obvious at first glance. Rabies risk, while uncommon with domestic pets, also needs to be assessed based on the animal’s vaccination status.

The Hidden Problem of Tooth Fragments

One complication of lip trauma that gets overlooked surprisingly often involves broken teeth. When a blow to the face fractures an upper front tooth, part of that tooth can be driven into the lower lip at the moment of impact and become embedded in the soft tissue. These fragments are not always easy to spot during a clinical exam, especially when there is swelling and bleeding.

If a tooth fragment is left inside the lip, it can cause chronic infection, a foreign-body reaction, discoloration of the overlying skin, and disfiguring scarring. The recommendation is to take radiographs of the soft tissue before closing any lip wound associated with dental trauma to rule out embedded fragments.
11
PubMed Central. 
Tooth fragment embedded in the lower lip for 10 months following dentoalveolar trauma: A case report with literature review
 In some cases, a retained fragment is discovered months later when it triggers symptoms or shows up on an unrelated X-ray.
12
PubMed. 
Tooth fragment embedded in the lower lip after dental trauma: case reports
 In pediatric cases, the fragment can sometimes be surgically retrieved and reattached to the broken tooth using adhesive techniques.
13
PubMed Central. 
Dental fragment embedded in the lower lip after facial trauma: Brief review literature and report of a case

The practical takeaway: if a lip injury happens alongside a chipped or broken tooth, mention the dental injury to the treating clinician even if the lip wound seems like the bigger problem. A quick X-ray could save a lot of trouble down the road.

Lip Injuries in Children

Falls are the leading cause of lip lacerations in children, and the lower lip gets hit disproportionately often because of the way kids land face-first. Parents frequently face the question of whether their child’s lip wound needs stitches or can be managed at home, and clinicians face a parallel question about how to close the wound with minimal distress.

Tissue adhesive (medical-grade skin glue) has become an increasingly popular alternative to sutures for facial lacerations in children. A study comparing the two methods for facial wounds found that cosmetic outcomes were similar between tissue adhesive and sutures, but children treated with glue reported significantly less pain and their families reported greater satisfaction with the experience.
14
PubMed Central. 
Comparative Evaluation of Tissue Adhesives and Sutures in the Management of Facial Laceration Wounds in Children
 Complication rates for wound opening and infection were comparable between the two approaches.

That said, tissue adhesive has limitations. It does not work well for wounds under tension, full-thickness lip lacerations, or wounds that cross the vermilion border where precise alignment is critical. For those injuries, sutures remain the standard. The choice often comes down to wound characteristics rather than the child’s preference, though when glue is appropriate, it spares the child the experience of needles and stitches.

Numbness and Nerve Recovery After Lip Trauma

Significant lip injuries, especially those involving the lower lip, can damage branches of the trigeminal nerve that provide sensation to the lip and chin. The result is numbness, tingling, or altered sensation that can persist long after the wound itself has healed. This is understandably alarming, but the news is generally encouraging.

Research on sensory recovery after trigeminal nerve injury shows that sensation returns in a predictable sequence. Simple touch perception and the ability to feel the direction of a brushstroke recover first, often within weeks. Pain and temperature sensation follow. Fine spatial discrimination, the ability to tell apart closely spaced points on the skin, recovers last and can take many months.
15
Brain. 
A psychophysical study of the mechanisms of sensory recovery following nerve injury in humans
 Animal research suggests that serotonin activity in the nerve pathways plays a role in speeding this recovery process.
16
PubMed Central. 
Serotonin promotes lip sensory recovery after inferior alveolar nerve transection via histone serotonylation

When nerve damage is severe enough to require microsurgical repair, about a third of patients regain full sensation, over half regain what is classified as useful sensory function, and roughly one in seven shows no meaningful recovery after a year.
17
Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery. 
Microsurgical Repair of Peripheral Trigeminal Nerve Injuries From Maxillofacial Trauma
 For most lip lacerations that do not involve deep nerve transection, the prognosis for sensory recovery is considerably better than these surgical cases. If you notice persistent numbness weeks after a lip injury, bring it up with your clinician, as early assessment can guide whether watchful waiting or intervention is more appropriate.

Managing Scars After Lip Wounds

Even with skilled repair, scars on and around the lip are a concern because the area is so visible. The lip’s healing advantages reduce but do not eliminate scarring on the outer skin surface, and any wound that crosses the vermilion border has the potential for a noticeable scar line.

Silicone-based scar treatments are the most widely studied non-surgical option. Silicone gel, applied topically once the wound has f

CONTENT:
Inhalation injuries occur when harmful substances enter your lungs and cause inflammation, irritation, or damage to your respiratory system. 
Some injuries are immediate, while others develop over time as a result of repeated exposure. There are two main types of inhalation injuries: thermal and chemical.
Inhaling hot gases or smoke can damage the upper respiratory tract (mouth, throat, and windpipe). Toxic chemicals such as chlorine or ammonia can cause burns, inflammation, and long-term lung damage.
Understanding what can cause an inhalation injury
Inhaling 
smoke
 or 
pollutants
, especially during 
wildfires
 or on days with high ozone levels, can damage your lungs over time.
Common activities that can increase your risk of inhalation injury include:
Cooking:
 Smoke, steam, or 
fumes
 in an inadequately ventilated kitchen can irritate your airways.
Cleaning:
 Household 
cleaning products
 containing harsh chemicals, such as bleach or ammonia, can release toxic fumes.
Renovations:
 Renovation projects that involve 
painting
, sanding, or using 
adhesives
 can release harmful fumes and particles into the air.
You may be more likely to develop an inhalation injury if you work in certain industries, such as:
Construction:
 Exposure to dust, 
asbestos
, or welding fumes can damage your 
respiratory system
.
Emergency response:
 When exposed to fire and smoke, firefighters and other first responders risk inhaling toxic gases such as 
carbon monoxide
 and 
hydrogen cyanide
.
Manufacturing:
 Inhaling toxic gases or fumes from chemicals used in manufacturing can cause long-term respiratory damage.
Common symptoms of an inhalation injury
Although symptoms vary depending on the substance inhaled and the extent of exposure, they generally include:
chest pain or tightness
coughing
hoarseness
shortness of breath
throat swelling
Seek emergency medical attention if you develop:
confusion
difficulty breathing
dizziness
loss of consciousness
throat swelling so severe that it begins to obstruct your airway
Diagnosing an inhalation injury
A healthcare professional will start by asking about the type and duration of exposure.
Next, they’ll 
assess your breathing
, listen for abnormal lung sounds, and check for signs of airway damage, such as swelling or soot around your mouth and nose.
They may order one or more of the following types of tests:
Imaging tests:
 Chest 
X-rays
 or 
CT scans
 may be used to check for lung damage, fluid in your lungs, or other signs of injury.
Blood tests:
 In cases of suspected carbon monoxide poisoning, 
blood tests
 can measure your levels of carboxyhemoglobin, indicating how much carbon monoxide is in your system.
Pulmonary function tests:
 These tests help assess the impact of inhalation injury on 
lung function
, especially if there is concern about long-term respiratory symptoms.
Bronchoscopy:
 In severe cases, healthcare professionals may perform a 
bronchoscopy
 to see the damage in your lungs and airways.
Treatment for an inhalation injury depends on the severity
Depending on the type of injury, a healthcare professional might prescribe 
bronchodilators
 to open your airways, 
corticosteroids
 to reduce inflammation, or 
antibiotics
 to prevent or treat infections.
For injuries involving 
oxygen deprivation
, breathing in 100% oxygen through a mask or via a 
hyperbaric chamber
 can help remove toxins from your bloodstream and restore oxygen levels.
Intravenous fluids may be used to help restore your blood pressure and keep you hydrated while your body heals.
In severe cases, a healthcare professional may insert a tube into your windpipe to help you breathe. 
Mechanical ventilation
 may be necessary if your lungs cannot function properly on their own.
Ongoing care may include 
respiratory therapy
, physical therapy, and long-term monitoring for complications.
Potential complications associated with inhalation injury
Depending on the severity and type of exposure, inhalation injuries can lead to several complications, such as:
Infection:
 The damage caused by inhalation injuries can increase the risk of 
bacterial or viral infections
 in your lungs. Pneumonia is a common complication of severe inhalation injuries.
Pulmonary edema:
 Inhalation injuries from hot gases or chemicals can lead to 
swelling and fluid buildup
 in the air sacs of your lungs.
Fibrosis:
 The healing process may lead to 
fibrosis
 (scarring), which can reduce lung function and cause long-term breathing difficulties.
Chronic respiratory conditions:
 Long-term exposure, especially in occupational settings, can result in conditions such as 
chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD)
, asthma, or interstitial lung disease.
Respiratory failure:
 If your lungs are severely damaged by toxic chemicals or smoke, they may not be able to provide enough oxygen to your body. This can be life threatening and may require mechanical ventilation.
How to prevent inhalation injury at home and in the workplace
You can install smoke detectors, maintain fire extinguishers, and create an emergency escape plan to reduce the risk of smoke inhalation in the event of a fire.
Proper 
ventilation in your home
 or workplace can reduce the buildup of fumes or smoke. To 
improve air quality
, use exhaust fans, open windows, and install air purifiers.
When working with potentially harmful substances at home or in a hazardous job, always wear the appropriate personal protective equipment, such as a 
face mask or respirator
, to filter out toxic substances.
The bottom line
Inhalation injuries can happen in any environment, including your home or workplace.
If you experience symptoms of an inhalation injury, it’s important to seek medical care as soon as possible. Prompt diagnosis and treatment can help prevent long-term complications and promote a faster recovery.

Handling Inhalation Injuries: Smoke, Steam, and Toxic Fumes

Breathing difficulties after smoke, steam, or toxic fume exposure? Inhalation injuries can damage your airway and lungs within minutes, making emergency care essential for restoring oxygen levels and preventing complications.

Learn the signs and symptoms of inhalation injury and when it’s time to go to the ER for life-saving treatment.

What Is an Inhalation Injury?

An inhalation injury occurs when smoke, steam, or toxic gases damage your airway or lungs. Injuries can range from mild irritation to life-threatening breathing problems.

Seeking emergency room smoke inhalation treatment is essential for children, older adults, and anyone with preexisting lung conditions.

Common Causes: Smoke, Steam, and Toxic Fumes

The most common causes of inhalation injuries include:

Smoke inhalation injury
 from house fires or accidents.

Steam inhalation injury
 from saunas, hot showers, or workplace accidents.

Toxic

fume exposure
 from chemicals, cleaning products, or industrial gases.

Even brief exposure can harm your lungs. It’s important to recognize the signs early to prevent complications or permanent damage.

How Inhalation Injuries Happen

You can suffer an inhalation injury when smoke, steam, or toxic fumes enter your airway and lungs. Here’s why:

Heat from steam or smoke can burn delicate nose and throat tissues.

Toxic fumes from chemicals can irritate and inflame the respiratory system.

Any exposure to a fire, industrial accident, or steam mishap can seriously damage tissues and airways, triggering breathing problems.

Why These Injuries Can Be Life-Threatening

Any damage to the airways or lungs can trigger breathing difficulties, low oxygen levels, and respiratory emergencies. Complications can escalate silently, making early recognition and immediate ER care essential for preventing long-term harm or life-threatening consequences.

Signs and Symptoms of Inhalation Injuries: Early Warning Signs

Persistent coughing or wheezing.

Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing.

Facial or throat irritation.

Soot or ash in the mouth, nose, or on clothing.

Symptoms of Toxic Fume Inhalation

Dizziness, headache, or nausea.

Burning sensation in the eyes, nostrils, or throat.

Coughing or chest tightness.

Confusion.

Steam Inhalation Burn Symptoms

Coughing or wheezing.

Hoarseness or difficulty speaking.

Swelling or irritation of the airway.

Redness or blistering inside the nose or mouth.

When to Go to the ER for an Inhalation Injury

Emergency Symptoms That Require Immediate Attention

If you or a loved one is experiencing one or more of the following symptoms, seek immediate medical treatment for steam inhalation:

Persistent coughing, wheezing, or difficulty breathing.

Facial or upper airway burns.

Confusion, dizziness, or chest pain.

Soot and swelling around the mouth and nose.

Why Delaying ER Treatment Can Be Dangerous

If you’ve been exposed to fire, intense heat from steam, or toxic chemicals, don’t shrug off throat irritation, coughing, wheezing, dizziness, or headaches.

These can be a warning sign of airway swelling and lung injury. 
According to the National Center for Biotechnology Information
, delaying emergency treatment for smoke inhalation injuries can put you at serious risk for respiratory failure or long-term lung damage.

ER vs. Urgent Care for Breathing Injuries

Most urgent care centers are not equipped to treat severe airway breathing emergencies, and when you’re struggling, every moment counts.

The board-certified physicians at 
Prestige ER
 are trained in the rapid diagnosis and treatment of inhalation injuries to protect you from severe complications and help you feel better fast.

Emergency Treatment for Inhalation Injuries

Here is what you can expect in the ER for inhalation injuries. Our treatments focus on restoring breathing and protecting the airway. Depending on the severity of your condition, you may receive:

Oxygen therapy
 to bring oxygen levels back to normal.

Airway management
 to relieve swelling and keep the airway open.

Specialized emergency care
 for toxic exposure and steam inhalation burns, which may include:
Medication.
Bronchodilators and inhalers.

Advanced lung monitoring.

Protect yourself from hidden or worsening damage by addressing your symptoms with professional medical care right away.

Long-Term Risks and Recovery

Lung Damage from Smoke or Fumes

Breathing in smoke or toxic chemicals can lead to permanent damage, such as:

Lung scarring.

Chronic cough.

Reduced breathing capacity.

Long-term sensitivity to irritants.

Burn Complications from Steam Inhalation Injuries

Steam inhalation can burn delicate airway tissue in the nose and throat, leading to swelling and infection during recovery.

Follow-Up Care After Emergency Treatment

Lung, airway, and tissue damage may not appear right away, which is why ongoing monitoring and follow-up care after emergency treatment for steam burns, chemical burns, and smoke inhalation is critical.

Aftercare may include one or more of the following to restore strength and prevent long-term complications:

Follow-up visits.

Lung function tests.

Wound care.

Breathing therapy.

Pulmonary rehab.

Why Choose Prestige ER for Inhalation Injury Care

Prestige ER provides fast, expert treatment for smoke inhalation injuries. Our 
emergency room services
 include:

24/7 emergency services for smoke and steam injuries.

Rapid diagnosis and advanced respiratory report.

Board-certified ER physicians on-site 24/7.

Expert staff trained in burn and toxic exposure care.

Visit your nearest 
location
 for fast, compassionate treatment for a broad range of 
medical emergencies
.

Summary
Inhalation injury occurs when noxious stimuli such as heat, gases, or particulate matter come into contact with the respiratory system.
Residential fires and workplace accidents are common events that lead to inhalation injury.
Pathophysiology includes thermal injury, systemic absorption of toxic compounds, and direct cellular injury.
Clinical manifestations include upper airway obstruction, carbon monoxide poisoning, airflow obstruction, and acute respiratory distress syndrome.
Therapy is largely supportive, although targeted therapies are the subject of active investigation.
Long-term sequelae and complications are common.
Definition
Inhalation injury is a spectrum of clinical disease that occurs when the respiratory system is exposed to extreme heat or toxic substances.

TITLE: 7 signs of inhalation injury that trauma nurses should be ...
SOURCE_DOMAIN: trauma-news.com
SOURCE_URL: https://trauma-news.com/2023/08/7-signs-of-inhalation-injury-that-trauma-nurses-should-be-aware-of/
AUTHORITY_SCORE: 3/10
RETRIEVED_AT: 2026-11-22T17:31:45.196150+09:00
SEARCH_SNIPPET:


CONTENT:
Inhalation injuries occur when respiratory tissue is damaged by heat, smoke or chemicals. More than three-quarters (77%) of burn victim deaths are due to pulmonary complications from inhalation injuries.

Trauma and emergency nurses should know the signs that inhalation injury might be present and understand the symptoms of inhalation-related problems.

1. Facial burns

Facial burns are common in patients with inhalation injury. Burns of the lips, tongue and mouth and singeing of the eyebrows may be evident. Patients should also be assessed for singeing of the nasal hair and burns of the nasal mucosa.

2. Painful swallowing

Painful swallowing after smoke exposure could indicate a possible inhalation injury. Inhalation burn may also be indicated by soot in the oropharynx and airways.

3. Difficulty breathing and other signs of upper airway injury

Upper airway injury is defined as injury above the vocal cords. Signs may include abnormal redness of the mucous membrane (erythema), ulceration and edema. Symptoms may include stridor (abnormal high-pitched breath sounds), hoarseness and difficulty breathing, which can lead to respiratory fatigue. In addition, damage to the cilia of the upper airway can lead to ineffective airway clearance.

4. Wheezing, coughing and other signs of tracheobronchial injury

Injury to the tracheobronchial tree can be caused by the inhalation of steam, chemicals or toxic gases. Symptoms may include wheezing, coughing, hypoventilation and erythema. Other indicators can include lung collapse (atelectasis) and soot in the secretions. In addition, smoke inhalation can cause local nerve damage, leading to bronchoconstriction.

5. Hypoxia and other signs of parenchymal injury

Parenchymal injury is injury to the alveoli, alveolar ducts and/or bronchioles. Damage to these parenchymal tissues can lead to pulmonary edema and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

Parenchymal tissue damage can be delayed due to the decrease in arterial oxygen. Signs can include atelectasis, alveolar collapse and hypoxia.

Clinical findings associated with ARDS include increased secretions, increased or rapid respirations, and decreased oxygen saturation. There may also be increased patchy infiltrates on chest radiographs.

6. Headache and other signs of carbon monoxide poisoning

Among patients who die from inhalation injuries, the most frequent cause of death is carbon monoxide (CO) poisoning. CO poisoning should be an assumed diagnosis in patients with inhalation injuries.

For patients with CO exposure, symptoms become more severe as the patient’s carboxyhemoglobin level increases.

Carboxyhemoglobin level

Typical symptoms

0 to 10%

Usually no symptoms

10% to 20%

Mild headache, dyspnea

20% to 30%

Throbbing headache, impaired concentration

30% to 40%

Severe headache, impaired thinking

40% to 50%

Confusion, lethargy, syncope

50% to 60%

Respiratory failure, seizure

60% to 70%

Coma, death

Trauma and emergency nurses should be aware that oxygen administration may create falsely low carboxyhemoglobin levels. In addition, pulse oximetry should 
not
 be used to evaluate inhalation injuries or the presence of CO poisoning because it cannot detect the difference between carboxyhemoglobin and normal oxyhemoglobin. In fact, pulse oximetry may be falsely elevated during CO exposure.

7. Decreased consciousness and other symptoms of cyanide poisoning

The symptoms of hydrogen cyanide (HCN) toxicity are nonspecific, making cyanide poisoning difficult to diagnose. Since HCN is caused by the combustion of plastics and other common materials, it is common in fire scenes. For that reason, cyanide poisoning should be considered in all patients being treated for smoke inhalation.

Patients affected by cyanide toxicity may exhibit:

Decreased level of consciousness

Cardiac arrest, cardiac decompensation and/or other cardiovascular symptoms

Hyperpnea (abnormally deep breathing) and/or hyperventilation

Seizures and/or dystonia

Coma

Hypothermia

What is Hypothermia?

Hypothermia is a potentially life-threatening, cold-related emergency that occurs when the body loses heat faster than it can produce heat, causing the core body temperature to fall below 95° F (35° C). Typically, the person experiences exposed to cold air temperatures, cold water or both. Hypothermia can also occur when the weather is not cold due to prolonged exposure in a wet or windy environment, wet clothes or sweating.

Signs and symptoms include:

Shivering, then lack of shivering

Pale and cold to touch

Disorientation, indifference, confusion

Glassy stare

Unresponsiveness

Slow or no breathing

Slow or no heart rate

Stiff body with rigid muscles

Find a Class

Emergency Steps

1

Check the scene safety, form an initial impression, obtain consent and put on PPE, as appropriate.

2

Check for signs and symptoms.

Disorientation, confusion or indifference*

Glassy stare*

Loss of ability to shiver as condition worsens*

Slowly of or no breathing*

Unresponsiveness*

Slowing of or no heart rate*

Body stiffening with ridged muscles*

Shivering

Pale skin

Cold to the touch

*Note: Signs and symptoms with a * require immediate emergency medical treatment.

3

Call 9-1-1 and get equipment if the person requires immediate emergency medical treatment.

4

Give Care.

General Care: Hypothermia

Rewarm the person slowly.


Rapid rewarming can lead to dangerous heart rhythms.

Move the person to a warmer place.

Remove wet clothes.

Dry the person.

Help the person put on dry clothing, including hat, gloves and socks, if available.

Wrap the person in dry blankets and plastic sheeting, if available.

Cover the person’s head.

Position the person as appropriate near a heat source or apply heating pads or hot water bottles filled with warm water to the body (if far from medical care).

Wrap heating pads or hot water bottles in thin, dry cloths to protect the person’s skin.

Offer small sips of a warm, non-caffeinated liquid if alert and can swallow. Examples include broth, warm water.

Continue checking them as appropriate to determine if additional care is needed.

Give care for shock, if necessary.

Reassure person you will help and that EMS has been called (if appropriate).

Watch for changes in condition, including breathing and responsiveness, and give care as appropriate.


Be prepared to give CPR or compression-only CPR based on level of training and use an AED when available if the person becomes unresponsive and is not breathing (cardiac arrest).

Hypothermia FAQs

How can hypothermia be prevented?

Dressing in layers can help to protect you against exposure illness from cold temperatures. A base layer, next to your skin, helps to regulate body temperature by wicking (i.e., absorbing or drawing away) sweat. Silk, merino wool and certain synthetics are best at wicking.

Cotton is not a good choice because it traps moisture. The middle layer acts as insulation, keeping you warm by trapping warm air close to your body. Natural fibers (wool and goose down) and synthetic fleece are excellent insulators. The outer layer protects from wind, rain or snow. For cold weather, this layer should be waterproof and “breathable.”

To stay warm, also wear:

A hat

A scarf/knit mask covering the face & mouth

Sleeves that are snug at the wrist

Mittens (warmer than gloves)

Water-resistant boots

Can I give a person with hypothermia an alcoholic drink to help warm them up?

No. Never give alcohol to a person who has hypothermia. Although alcohol may temporarily make the person feel warmer, it actually increases loss of body heat. You should also avoid giving a person who has hypothermia beverages containing caffeine, because caffeine promotes fluid loss and can lead to dehydration.

What else can I use if I don't have a blanket?

You could use additional clothing, sheets or towels for warming. If needed, you can use plastic sheeting, newspaper or cardboard. You can also use heating pads and hot water bottles to warm the person. However, wrap them in thin, dry cloth to protect the skin.

Get out of the cold immediately if the signals of hypothermia or frostbite appear. Hypothermia is the cooling of the body caused by the failure of the body’s warming system. The goals of first aid are to restore normal body temperature and to care for any conditions while waiting for EMS personnel. What are the signs of hypothermia?

CONTENT:
How to Identify and Treat
Hypothermia and Frostbite

How to Identify and Treat
Hypothermia and Frostbite

Frostbite and hypothermia are cold-related emergencies that may quickly become life or limb threatening.

Take these steps to avoid frostbite and hypothermia:

Be aware of the wind chill. Dress appropriately and avoid staying in the cold too long. Wear a hat and gloves when appropriate with layers of clothing. Avoid unnecessary exposure of any part of the body to the cold.
Drink plenty of warm fluids or warm water but avoid caffeine and alcohol. Stay active to maintain body heat.
Take frequent breaks from the cold.
Get out of the cold immediately if the signals of hypothermia or frostbite appear.

How to Identify and Treat Hypothermia

Hypothermia is the cooling of the body caused by the failure of the body’s warming system. 

The goals of first aid are to restore normal body temperature and to care for any conditions while waiting for EMS personnel.

What are the signs of hypothermia?

Shivering
Numbness or weakness
Glassy stare
Apathy or impaired judgment
Loss of consciousness

What should you do if someone has hypothermia?

CALL 9-1-1 or the local emergency number.
Gently move the person to a warm place.
Monitor breathing and circulation.
Give rescue breathing and CPR if needed.
Remove any wet clothing and dry the person.
Warm the person slowly by wrapping in blankets or by putting dry clothing on the person.
Hot water bottles and chemical hot packs may be used when first wrapped in a towel or blanket before applying. Do not warm the person too quickly, such as by immersing him or her in warm water.
Warm the core first (trunk, abdomen), not the extremities (hands, feet).

How to Identify and Treat Frostbite

Frostbite is the freezing of a specific body part such as fingers, toes, the nose or earlobes.

What are the signs of frostbite?

Lack of feeling in the affected area
Skin that appears waxy, is cold to the touch, or is discolored (flushed, white or gray, yellow or blue)

What should you do if someone has frostbite?

Move the person to a warm place.
Handle the area gently; never rub the affected area.
Warm gently by soaking the affected area in warm. water (100–105 degrees F) until it appears red and feels warm.
Loosely bandage the area with dry, sterile dressings.
If the person’s fingers or toes are frostbitten, place dry, sterile gauze between them to keep them separated.
Avoid breaking any blisters.
Do not allow the affected area to refreeze.
Seek professional medical care as soon as possible.

Aug 25, 2026 · Hypothermia (abnormally low body temperature) is a dangerous condition that can happen when a person is exposed to extremely cold temperatures. Stay safe this winter by learning more about hypothermia, including who is most at risk, signs and symptoms, and what to do if someone develops hypothermia.

CONTENT:
Preventing Hypothermia

 For Everyone 

 Aug. 25, 2026 

Español

Key points

Hypothermia (abnormally low body temperature) is a dangerous condition that can happen when a person is exposed to extremely cold temperatures.

Stay safe this winter by learning more about hypothermia, including who is most at risk, signs and symptoms, and what to do if someone develops hypothermia.

Overview

Stay safe this winter by learning more about hypothermia, including who is most at risk, signs and symptoms, and what to do if someone develops hypothermia.

What is hypothermia?

Hypothermia can happen when a person is exposed to very cold temperature for a long period of time. When exposed to cold temperatures, your body begins to lose heat faster than it's produced. Lengthy exposures will eventually use up your body's stored energy, which leads to lower body temperature.

Body temperature that is too low affects the brain, making the victim unable to think clearly or move well. This makes hypothermia especially dangerous, because a person may not know that it's happening and won't be able to do anything about it.

While hypothermia is most likely at very cold temperatures, it can occur even at cool temperatures (above 40°F) if a person becomes chilled from rain, sweat, or submersion in cold water.

Risk factors

Victims of hypothermia are often:

Older adults with inadequate food, clothing, or heating

Babies sleeping in cold bedrooms

People who remain outdoors for long periods—people experiencing homelessness, hikers, hunters, etc.

People who drink alcohol or use illicit drugs.

What to look out for

The following are warnings signs of hypothermia:

 Adults 

Shivering
Exhaustion or feeling very tired
Confusion
Fumbling hands
Memory loss
Slurred speech
Drowsiness

 Babies 

Bright red, cold skin
Very low energy

Don't wait— take action

In cold temperatures, your body begins to lose heat faster than it can be produced, which can lead to serious health problems.

Avoid, spot, treat frostbite & hypothermia.

In cold temperatures, your body begins to lose heat faster than it can be produced, which can lead to serious health problems.

Avoid

When the weather is extremely cold, try to stay indoors. If you must go outside, dress properly and know who is at high risk for hypothermia or frostbite. When going outside be sure to wear: a scarf or knit mask that covers face and mouth; a hat; mittens of gloves; a water-resistant coat; water-resistant boots; and several layers of loose-fitting clothing. 

When going outside in winter make sure body parts most often affected by frostbite are covered in warm, dry clothing: nose, ears, toes, cheeks, chin, and fingers. 

Know who is at high risk: older adults without proper food, clothing, or heating; people who stay outdoors for long periods (homeless, hikers, hunters, etc.); people who drink alcohol in excess or use illicit drugs; and babies sleeping in cold rooms. 

Spot

Frostbite

 A victim is often unaware of frostbite because frozen tissue is numb. 

Signs & Symptoms: Redness or pain in any skin area may be the first sign of frostbite. Other signs include: a white or grayish-yellow skin area; skin that feels unusually firm or waxy; and numbness

Hypothermia

Hypothermia often occurs at very cold temperatures, but can occur at cool temperatures (above 40 degrees Fahrenheit), if a person is wet (from rain, sweat, or cold water) and becomes chilled. 

Signs & Symptoms

Adults: shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech, drowsiness.

Infants: bright red, cold skin, and very low energy. 

If a person's temperature is below 95 degrees get medical attention immediately. 

Treat

If a person is experiencing hypothermia or frostbite...

1) Seek medical attention as soon as possible. 

2) Get them into a warm room or shelter. 

3) Remove any wet clothing. 

4) Warm them under dry layers of blankets and clothing. 

5) Place areas affected by frostbite in warm-to-touch water. 

Frostbite Caut!on

Since skin may be numb, victims of frostbite can harm themselves further. Use caution when treating frostbite and: 

1) Unless necessary, do not walk on feet or toes with frostbite. 

2) Do not use a fireplace, heat lamp, radiator, or stove for warming. 

3) Do not use a heating pad or electric blanket for warming. 

4) Do not rub or massage areas with frostbite. 
Show Text Description

Download Infographic

Hypothermia is a medical emergency. If you notice any of the above signs, take the person's temperature. If it is below 95° F, get medical attention immediately!

If you are not able to get medical help right away, try to warm the person up.

Get the person into a warm room or shelter.

Remove any wet clothing the person is wearing.

Warm the center of the person's body—chest, neck, head, and groin—using an electric blanket, if available. You can also use skin-to-skin contact under loose, dry layers of blankets, clothing, towels, or sheets.

Warm drinks can help increase body temperature, but do not give alcoholic drinks. Do not try to give beverages to an unconscious person.

After body temperature has increased, keep the person dry and wrap their body, including their head and neck, in a warm blanket.

Get the person proper medical attention as soon as possible.

Severe hypothermia

A person with severe hypothermia may be unconscious and may not seem to have a pulse or to be breathing. 

In this case, handle the person gently, and get emergency assistance immediately.

Perform CPR, even if the person appears dead. CPR should continue until the person responds or medical aid becomes available. Keep warming the person while performing CPR. In some cases, hypothermia victims who appear to be dead can be successfully resuscitated.

AUTHORITY_SCORE: 8/10

SEARCH_SNIPPET:
Apr 16, 2024 · When to seek emergency help If you suspect someone has hypothermia, call 911 or your local emergency number.

CONTENT:
Hypothermia: First aid
By Mayo Clinic Staff
April 16, 2024
Overview

Hypothermia happens when the body loses heat faster than it can produce heat and the body temperature falls below 95 degrees Fahrenheit (35 degrees Celsius). Left untreated, it can be life-threatening.

Hypothermia is often caused by exposure to cold weather or immersion in cold water. Ongoing exposure to cool indoor temperatures also can cause hypothermia, especially in older adults and babies. Being exhausted or dehydrated increases the risk of hypothermia.

When to seek emergency help

If you suspect someone has hypothermia, 
call 911 or your local emergency number.

Symptoms

Symptoms of hypothermia usually develop slowly and may include:

Shivering, though this may stop as body temperature drops.

Slurred speech or mumbling.

Slow, shallow breathing.

Weak pulse.

Clumsiness or lack of coordination.

Drowsiness or very low energy.

Confusion or memory loss.

Loss of consciousness.

In infants, bright red, cold skin.

Treatment

To help someone with hypothermia, take these steps immediately:

Gently move the person out of the cold. If going indoors isn't possible, protect the person from the wind, especially around the neck and head. Insulate the individual from the cold ground, such as by laying a blanket underneath the person.

Gently remove wet clothing. Replace wet things with warm, dry coats or blankets.

If further warming is needed, do so gradually and focus on the center of the body. For example, apply warm, dry compresses to the neck, chest and groin. The CDC says that another option is using an electric blanket, if available. If a hot water bottle or chemical hot pack is used, first wrap it in a towel before applying.

Offer the person warm, sweet, nonalcoholic drinks.

Begin CPR if the person shows no signs of life, such as breathing, coughing or movement.

What to avoid

Do not rewarm the person too quickly, such as with a heating lamp or hot bath.

Don't attempt to warm the arms and legs. Heating or massaging the limbs can stress the heart and lungs.

Don't give the person alcohol or cigarettes. Alcohol hinders the rewarming process, and tobacco products interfere with circulation that is needed for rewarming.

TITLE: Hypothermia Symptoms and First Aid | St John Ambulance
SOURCE_DOMAIN: sja.org.uk
SOURCE_URL: https://www.sja.org.uk/first-aid-advice/hypothermia/
AUTHORITY_SCORE: 3/10

SEARCH_SNIPPET:
Find first aid information from St John Ambulance about hypothermia, including a definition of hypothermia, as well as causes, symptoms and treatment.

CONTENT:
Hypothermia
Dr Lynn Thomas, OStJ, BSc, MB.BS, MA, FRCP
Clinically reviewed:

28/04/2025
Hypothermia can become life threatening quickly, so it’s important to treat it straight away.  Find out what to look for and how to perform first aid.
Emergency advice
What is hypothermia?
Hypothermia is a condition that occurs when someone’s body temperature drops below 35°C (95°F). Normal body temperature is around 37°C (98. 6°F). Hypothermia can become life threatening quickly, so it’s important to treat someone with hypothermia straight away.
Signs and symptoms
Look for:
shivering, cold and pale with dry skin  
unusually tired, confused, and irrational behaviour
reduced level of response
slow and shallow breathing 
slow and weakening pulse
A baby may:
be cold to touch
have mottled (blotchy) skin
be quiet and sleepy
be limp
refuse to feed
What to do if treating hypothermia outdoors
1
If the casualty is outside, try to get them indoors. If you are unable to get them indoors, try to take them to a sheltered place as quickly as possible, shielding the casualty from the wind.
2
Remove and replace any wet clothing and make sure their head is covered.
Do not give them your clothes - it is important for you to stay warm yourself.
3
Try to protect the casualty from the ground. Lay them on a thick layer of dry insulating material, such as pine branches, heather, or bracken. If possible, put them in a dry sleeping bag or cover them with blankets. If available, wrap them in a foil survival blanket. You can use your own body to shelter them and keep them warm.
4
Call 999 or 112 for emergency help.
Do not leave the casualty alone. Somebody must be with them at all times. If you are in a remote area and cannot call for emergency help, send two people to get help together.
5
If the casualty is fully alert, offer them warm drinks and high energy food such as chocolate.
6
Monitor their breathing and level of responsiveness while waiting for help to arrive.
What to do if treating hypothermia indoors
1
If you are indoors, cover the casualty with layers of blankets and warm the room to about 25°C (77°F).
Do not place any direct heat such as hot water bottles or fires near a casualty as this can cause burns.
2
Give them something warm to drink, like soup, and high-energy food, like chocolate.
Do not give the casualty alcohol in an attempt to warm them - it will make hypothermia worse.
3
If there is no obvious reason for the casualty to have hypothermia, seek medical advice. Hypothermia could be disguising a more serious illness such as a 
stroke
, 
heart attack
, or an underactive thyroid gland.
4
Monitor their breathing and level of responsiveness until they recover.

If you found this article helpful in any way, a donation of any size can help us reach more people with life-saving advice, expert care, and essential training.

DOCUMENT_ID: 02_006
SECTION: 02.24 Hypothermia and Cold Exposure
TITLE: Hypothermia First Aid: Symptoms and What to Do
SOURCE_DOMAIN: firstaidsafetytraining.com
SOURCE_URL: https://firstaidsafetytraining.com/hypothermia-prevention/
AUTHORITY_SCORE: 3/10
RETRIEVED_AT: 2026-11-22T17:31:45.196150+09:00
SEARCH_SNIPPET:
Hypothermia first aid explained. Learn the symptoms of hypothermia, how to warm someone safely, what not to do and when to call 999.

CONTENT:
Hypothermia first aid
 focuses on preventing further heat loss, getting the casualty somewhere sheltered, replacing wet clothing with dry insulation and getting medical help. Hypothermia occurs when the body’s temperature falls dangerously low and it can become life-threatening.

It is often associated with freezing winter weather, but hypothermia can develop in less extreme conditions too.

Cold wind, wet clothing, immersion in cold water, exhaustion and prolonged exposure can all contribute.

If you think someone has hypothermia, treat it seriously and get medical help.

What Is Hypothermia?

Hypothermia is a dangerous drop in body temperature.

Normal body temperature is around 37°C. The NHS defines hypothermia as a body temperature 
below 35°C
.

As the body cools, its normal functions begin to slow down.

This can affect:

the brain

breathing

circulation

coordination

judgement

consciousness

eventually, the heart

Hypothermia is therefore more than simply feeling very cold.

It is a medical emergency.

What Causes Hypothermia?

Hypothermia develops when the body loses heat faster than it can produce it.

Common causes include:

staying outside in cold weather for too long

inadequate clothing

wet clothing

falling into cold water

cold and windy conditions

prolonged exposure after an accident

living in a very cold home

exhaustion during outdoor activities

The risk is not determined by air temperature alone.

Wet clothing and wind can significantly increase heat loss.

Someone who becomes injured outdoors may also be particularly vulnerable because they are unable to keep moving or reach shelter.

What Are the Symptoms of Hypothermia?

Possible symptoms include:

shivering

cold skin

pale skin

blue or grey lips or skin

slurred speech

slow breathing

tiredness

confusion

As hypothermia becomes more severe, the casualty may become increasingly confused, drowsy or unresponsive.

Shivering may also reduce or stop as their condition becomes more serious.

Do not assume that somebody who has stopped shivering is getting warmer.

In a severely cold casualty, stopping shivering can be a warning sign.

Recognising Hypothermia in Different Skin Tones

Changes in skin colour can sometimes be more difficult to recognise depending on the casualty’s skin tone.

The NHS notes that blue or grey colour changes may be easier to see on the 
palms of the hands or soles of the feet
 in someone with black or brown skin.

Do not rely on skin colour alone.

Look at the whole casualty and consider symptoms such as:

shivering

cold skin

slurred speech

confusion

drowsiness

abnormal breathing

reduced responsiveness

Hypothermia First Aid: What Should You Do?

If you suspect hypothermia:

Call 999 or arrange urgent medical help.

Move the casualty somewhere sheltered if this can be done safely.

Protect them from wind and further cold exposure.

Remove wet clothing gently.

Replace wet clothing with dry clothing, blankets or a sleeping bag.

Cover their head.

Insulate them from the cold ground.

Give a warm non-alcoholic drink and sugary food only if they are fully awake and can swallow safely.

Stay with them and monitor their condition.

Avoid unnecessary handling, particularly if the casualty appears seriously affected.

Call 999 for Suspected Hypothermia

The NHS advises getting emergency medical help if you think someone has hypothermia.

Call 
999
 and ask for an ambulance if necessary.

Do not assume you can simply warm someone up and then send them home.

A significantly hypothermic casualty may need hospital assessment and treatment.

Tell the ambulance service:

what happened

how long the casualty may have been exposed

whether they became wet or were immersed in water

their current condition

whether their responsiveness or breathing has changed

Follow the call handler’s instructions.

Move the Casualty Somewhere Sheltered

Preventing further heat loss is an important part of 
hypothermia first aid
.

Where possible, move the casualty:

indoors

into a vehicle

into a tent or shelter

behind an effective windbreak

somewhere protected from rain, snow and wind

However, do not put yourself in danger trying to move someone from a hazardous location.

Call the emergency services if specialist rescue is required.

Remove Wet Clothing

Wet clothing can continue drawing heat away from the body.

If possible, gently remove wet clothing and replace it with:

dry clothing

blankets

towels

a sleeping bag

other suitable dry insulation

Protect the casualty from further exposure while doing this.

Avoid leaving them unnecessarily exposed while changing clothing.

Insulate the Casualty from the Ground

Heat can be lost through direct contact with a cold surface.

Do not simply wrap the top of the casualty while leaving them lying directly on cold ground.

Place suitable insulation underneath them where possible.

This might include:

blankets

sleeping mats

dry clothing

foam pads

other insulating materials

Current Resuscitation Council UK guidance specifically identifies 
ground isolation
 as part of preventing hypothermia.

Protect Them from the Wind

Wind can increase heat loss significantly.

Use available shelter or barriers to protect the casualty.

This might mean:

moving behind a wall

entering a shelter

using a tent

using a vehicle

creating a windbreak

Combine wind protection with dry insulation.

Should You Give Someone with Hypothermia a Hot Drink?

The NHS recommends a 
warm, non-alcoholic drink
 if the casualty is fully awake.

They may also be given sugary food, such as chocolate, if they are fully alert and able to eat safely.

Do not give food or drink to somebody who:

is significantly drowsy

is confused and cannot safely swallow

is becoming unresponsive

cannot protect their own airway

Never give alcohol.

Why Shouldn’t You Give Alcohol?

Alcohol can make someone feel warmer because blood vessels near the skin widen.

However, this can increase heat loss.

Alcohol can also impair judgement and affect someone’s ability to recognise how seriously cold they have become.

The NHS specifically advises 
not giving alcohol
 to someone with hypothermia.

Should You Put Someone with Hypothermia in a Hot Bath?

No.

Do 
not
 suddenly place someone with hypothermia into a hot bath or shower.

The NHS also advises against using:

hot water bottles

heat lamps

The aim for a first aider is to prevent further heat loss and allow safe rewarming while professional medical help is arranged.

Do not try to heat the casualty aggressively.

Should You Rub Their Arms and Legs?

No.

Do not vigorously rub or massage the casualty’s:

hands

feet

arms

legs

The NHS specifically advises against rubbing the limbs of someone with hypothermia.

Handle the casualty gently.

What If the Casualty Is Unresponsive?

An unresponsive hypothermic casualty requires urgent medical help.

Call 
999
 if this has not already been done.

Assess their breathing carefully.

Severe hypothermia can cause breathing and circulation to become extremely slow.

Current Resuscitation Council UK guidance advises healthcare and rescue responders to check for vital signs for up to one minute in an unconscious hypothermic casualty because they can be difficult to detect.

For a first aider, the priority is to call 999 promptly, follow the ambulance service’s instructions and be prepared to provide resuscitation if required.

What If Someone with Hypothermia Stops Breathing Normally?

If the casualty is unresponsive and you believe they are not breathing normally, follow the instructions of the ambulance service and begin CPR when indicated.

Use an AED if one is available and follow its prompts.

Do not assume somebody cannot survive simply because they are extremely cold and appear lifeless.

Severe hypothermia can produce very slow vital signs, and specialist resuscitation and rewarming techniques may be possible.

Continue following emergency service instructions until professional help takes over.

Our 
Basic Life Support guide
 explains the general principles of recognising cardiac arrest, CPR and AED use.

You can also read our 
Seven Steps of CPR
 guide.

Mild, Moderate and Severe Hypothermia

Hypothermia becomes increasingly dangerous as body temperature falls.

Current Resuscitation Council UK specialist guidance uses stages to help assess accidental hypothermia.

Mild Hypothermia

A casualty may still be:

conscious

alert

shivering

The estimated core temperature may be around 
35°C to 32°C
.

Moderate Hypothermia

The casualty’s consciousness may become impaired.

They may develop:

confusion

lethargy

reduced coordination

Shivering may reduce or stop.

The estimated core temperature may be around 
32°C to 28°C
.

Severe Hypothermia

At lower temperatures, the casualty may become unconscious and their breathing and circulation can become extremely slow.

This is a life-threatening emergency requiring specialist medical treatment and controlled rewarming.

Members of the public should not delay calling 999 while trying to determine a precise stage or temperature.

Can You Measure Someone’s Temperature?

A normal household thermometer may not be capable of accurately measuring very low core temperatures.

Specialist medical teams use appropriate low-reading equipment and suitable core-temperature measurement techniques.

Do not delay treatment while repeatedly trying to obtain a temperature.

If the casualty has been exposed to cold and has symptoms consistent with hypothermia, get medical help and begin preventing further heat loss.

Hypothermia After Falling into Cold Water

Cold-water immersion can cause several serious problems.

A casualty removed from cold water may continue to be at risk from:

breathing problems

drowning complications

hypothermia

reduced consciousness

cardiac arrest

Get emergency medical help.

Once the casualty has been removed from the water safely:

protect them from wind

remove wet clothing where appropriate

dry and insulate them

keep them off the cold ground

monitor responsiveness and breathing

Never put yourself at risk by entering dangerous water to attempt a rescue.

Our guide to the 
different types of drowning
 explains why someone rescued from water may still need urgent assessment.

Hypothermia in Babies and Children

Babies and young children can lose heat quickly.

The NHS advises that a baby with hypothermia may be:

cold to touch

floppy

unusually quiet

sleepy

unwilling to feed

Do not wait for obvious shivering.

If you think a baby or child has hypothermia, get urgent medical help.

Keep them dry, protected from the cold and appropriately insulated while waiting for assistance.

Parents, carers and people working with children can learn how to recognise and manage emergencies through practical 
Paediatric First Aid training
.

Who Is Most at Risk of Hypothermia?

Anyone exposed to cold conditions can become hypothermic.

Some people may be particularly vulnerable, including:

babies

young children

older people

people with certain health conditions

people living in inadequately heated homes

people who are wet

people who are exhausted

people affected by alcohol or drugs

outdoor workers

walkers and hikers

climbers

people participating in outdoor sport

people who have fallen into cold water

Someone who is injured and unable to move may also cool much more quickly than expected.

Hypothermia Can Happen Indoors

Hypothermia is not exclusively an outdoor emergency.

Someone can become dangerously cold inside an inadequately heated home.

Older or vulnerable people may be particularly at risk.

Signs such as:

confusion

unusual drowsiness

slurred speech

cold skin

slow breathing

should not simply be dismissed as tiredness or old age.

Consider the environment and get medical help if hypothermia is suspected.

Hypothermia in the Workplace

Some jobs expose workers to cold, wet or windy conditions.

These may include:

construction

agriculture

maritime work

outdoor maintenance

utilities

forestry

security

events

delivery work

other outdoor occupations

Employers should consider environmental exposure as part of their risk assessment.

Controls might include:

appropriate protective clothing

waterproof clothing

warm rest areas

suitable breaks

access to warm drinks

monitoring weather conditions

changing wet clothing

emergency arrangements

suitable first aid provision

Our guide to the 
legal requirement for first aid at work
 explains how workplace risks should influence first aid arrangements.

Preventing Hypothermia Outdoors

Prevention is much easier than treating a casualty who has become seriously cold.

Before outdoor activity:

check the weather forecast

wear suitable layers

carry waterproof clothing

take spare dry clothing

protect the head and extremities

carry emergency shelter where appropriate

take enough food and drink

plan the route

tell someone where you are going

carry suitable communication equipment

Adapt your equipment and planning to the environment and activity.

Why Wet Clothing Matters

Water conducts heat away from the body much more effectively than dry air.

This means a person who becomes soaked can cool rapidly, particularly when wind is also present.

Someone does not need to be standing in snow to develop hypothermia.

A combination of:

cold + wind + rain + exhaustion

can create a significant risk.

This is particularly important during outdoor activities and outdoor work in the UK.

Hypothermia and First Aid After an Injury

Preventing heat loss is important when treating an injured casualty outdoors, even when hypothermia was not the original problem.

Someone who is:

bleeding

injured

lying still

exhausted

wet

exposed to wind

can cool rapidly.

Once immediate life-threatening problems have been managed, protect the casualty from the environment.

Use dry insulation above and below them and provide shelter from wind and rain.

Hypothermia First Aid: What Not to Do

If you suspect hypothermia:

DO NOT use a hot bath.

DO NOT use a hot water bottle directly to rapidly heat them.

DO NOT use a heat lamp.

DO NOT rub their hands, feet, arms or legs.

DO NOT give them alcohol.

DO NOT give food or drink if they cannot swallow safely.

DO NOT leave them alone.

DO NOT assume that stopping shivering means they are getting better.

Instead, prevent further heat loss, handle them gently, get medical help and monitor their condition.

Hypothermia First Aid: What to Remember

The main 
hypothermia first aid
 principles are:

GET HELP

Hypothermia is a medical emergency. Call 999 or arrange urgent medical help.

GET THEM SHELTERED

Move them indoors or somewhere protected from the weather where possible.

REMOVE WET CLOTHING

Gently replace wet clothing with dry clothing and insulation.

KEEP THEM INSULATED

Use blankets, towels, sleeping bags or dry clothing.

Remember to insulate them from the cold ground an

Exertional Hypothermia/Heat Stroke

Exertional Hypothermia/heat stroke is the least common but most severe heat-related illness. It occurs when the body’s cooling system becomes completely overwhelmed and stops working. Exertional hyperthermia/heat stroke is a life-threatening emergency.

Find a Class

Emergency Steps

1

Check the scene safety, form an initial impression, obtain consent and put on PPE, as appropriate.

2

Check for signs and symptoms.

Moist, pale or flushed skin*

No or some sweating*

Rapid, shallow breathing*

Seizure*

Unresponsiveness*

Rapid, weak heartbeat*

Confusion*

Nausea or vomiting*

Headache or dizziness*

Weakness

Exhaustion

*Note: Signs and symptoms with a * require immediate emergency medical treatment.

3

Call 9-1-1 and get equipment if the person requires immediate emergency medical treatment.

4

Give Care.

Giving First Aid Care

Begin rapid cooling while waiting for EMS.

Preferred method: Immerse the person up to the neck in cold water for 15 minutes or until they are no longer confused.

If immersion is not possible, use a method such as: ice packs, ice sheets, cooling towels, cold shower, cooling vest, misting and fanning the person, or a combination of these.

Continue cooling them for 20 minutes, or until their condition improves or EMS personnel arrive.

Watch for changes in the person’s condition and give care as needed for other conditions found.

Heat Stroke FAQs

What environmental temperature is most likely to cause a heat-related illness? Are there other risk factors besides temperature?

Environmental temperatures that are greater than 100° F (38° C) increase risk. However, if someone is unaccustomed to labor or exercise in the heat, they can develop a heat-related illness at lower environmental temperatures. Other factors, such as humid air, inadequate fluid intake, heavy clothing and personal characteristics (e.g., the presence of certain medical conditions, taking certain medications and the person’s age, especially older adults and young children and infants) can increase the risk for heat-related illness.

Heat exhaustion: First aid
By Mayo Clinic Staff
April 16, 2024
Overview

Heat exhaustion is one of the heat-related syndromes. These syndromes vary in seriousness, ranging from mild to possibly life-threatening. Other types of heat-related illnesses include heat rash, heat cramps, heat syncope and heatstroke.

Heat exhaustion can happen when the body loses too much water or salt — usually because of heavy sweating or dehydration. It can begin suddenly or happen over time, usually after working, exercising or playing in the heat.

When to seek emergency help

Call 911 or your local emergency number if the affected person:

Faints.

Becomes agitated.

Is confused.

Has a seizure.

Is not able to drink.

Has a core body temperature – measured with a rectal thermometer – of 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius), which indicates heatstroke.

Symptoms

Heat exhaustion symptoms include:

Cool, moist skin with goose bumps when in the heat.

Heavy sweating.

Faintness.

Dizziness.

Fatigue.

Weak, rapid pulse.

Low blood pressure after standing up.

Muscle cramps.

Nausea or vomiting.

Headache.

Extreme thirst.

Mild confusion.

Decreased urine output.

Treatment

Untreated, heat exhaustion can lead to heatstroke, which is a life-threatening condition. If you suspect heat exhaustion, take these steps immediately:

Move the person out of the heat and into a shady or air-conditioned place.

Lay the person down and raise the legs and feet slightly.

Remove tight or heavy clothing.

Have the person sip chilled water, a sports drink containing electrolytes or another nonalcoholic beverage without caffeine.

Cool the person by spraying or sponging with cool water and fanning.

Monitor the person carefully.

Contact a healthcare professional if symptoms get worse or if the person doesn't improve after taking first-aid measures.

CONTENT:
Heatstroke: First aid
By Mayo Clinic Staff
May 29, 2024
Overview

Heatstroke happens when body temperature rises quickly and a person can't cool down. It can be life-threatening by causing damage to the brain and other vital organs. It may be caused by doing strenuous activity in the heat or by being in a hot place for too long. Heatstroke can happen without having any previous heat-related condition, such as heat exhaustion.

When to seek emergency help

If you suspect heatstroke, 
call 911 or your local emergency number
. Then move the person out of the heat right away.

Symptoms

Heatstroke symptoms include:

Fever of 104 degrees Fahrenheit (40 degrees Celsius) or greater.

Changes in mental status or behavior, such as confusion, agitation and slurred speech.

Hot, dry skin or heavy sweating.

Nausea and vomiting.

Flushed skin.

Rapid pulse.

Rapid breathing.

Headache.

Fainting.

Seizure.

Coma.

Treatment

For heatstroke, cool the person through whatever means available. For example:

Put the person in a cool tub of water or a cool shower.

Spray the person with a garden hose.

Sponge the person with cool water.

Fan the person while misting with cool water.

Place ice packs or cool, wet towels on the neck, armpits and groin.

Cover the person with cool, damp sheets.

If the person is conscious, offer chilled water, a sports drink containing electrolytes or another nonalcoholic beverage without caffeine.

Begin CPR if the person loses consciousness and shows no signs of circulation, such as breathing, coughing or movement.
